content: Flaxseed has specific dosing recommendations based on its intended use. For oral consumption, the typical dose is 1 tablespoon taken two to three times daily, or 15-50 grams per day. Alternatively, 15-30 milliliters taken orally once daily is equivalent to 200 milligrams of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) per day. For topical application, 30-50 grams can be used as needed. It is important to consume flaxseed with an adequate amount of fluid to prevent bowel obstruction. Flaxseed is used for various conditions, including chronic constipation, benign prostatic hyperplasia (when using flaxseed oil), cancer prevention, diabetes, diverticulitis, gastritis or enteritis, hypercholesterolemia, irritable bowel syndrome, menopausal symptoms, myocardial infarction prevention (when using flaxseed oil), skin inflammation, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) nephritis. It is considered possibly effective for managing diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, menopausal symptoms, and SLE nephritis. Flaxseed contains phytoestrogens, which may interact with other substances containing phytoestrogens through pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially increasing their effects. Caution and close monitoring are advised when combining flaxseed with other phytoestrogen-containing products. Adverse effects associated with flaxseed include allergic reactions, anaphylactoid reactions, diarrhea (particularly with flaxseed oil), and intestinal obstruction. Contraindications include conditions such as bowel obstruction, hormone-sensitive cancers (e.g., breast, ovarian, uterine), endometriosis, esophageal strictures, acute intestinal inflammation, uterine fibroids, and hypertriglyceridemia. Flaxseed oil may also pose risks for individuals with bleeding disorders. The safety of flaxseed during pregnancy and lactation has not been extensively studied. However, moderate consumption is believed to be beneficial, and its nutrients may support breast milk production. Pregnant and breastfeeding individuals should consult a healthcare professional before use. In general, flaxseed is considered acceptable during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
